extraction.title: Identifying hidden coalitions in the US House
extraction.document_type: Journal article (open access, CC BY 4.0). Metadata hint verified against the PDF front matter; no correction needed. Received 5 June 2021, accepted 3 September 2021.
extraction.coverage: Full text read in two chunks (all 682 text lines, front matter through references and licence block). All 58 annotation items in _annots/a93789ed82c1.json were read; all are Paul Goff highlights on pages 1-8 with empty content (no sticky-note text). Figures and SI tables are referenced but not in the text file, so figure content is taken from captions and prose only. The Supplementary Information is not in the source and was not read.
extraction.research_question: (1) Can globally optimal partitions of a signed network into k mutually divisive, internally cohesive clusters (generalized balance / k-clusterability) be computed for realistic social networks? (2) What is the smallest k that minimizes frustrated edges? (3) Does partitioning US House legislators by their signed collaboration and opposition ties fit the chamber better than partitioning by party, and what does the resulting structure say about legislative effectiveness?
extraction.theory: Generalized (k-) balance and clusterability theory (Davis 1967; Cartwright and Harary 1976), extending classic structural balance (Heider 1944; Cartwright and Harary 1956). A signed network is k-balanced if its nodes split into k coalitions with positive ties within and negative ties between. Distance from balance is the count of frustrated edges. Coalitions are clusters and need not be cohesive or collaborating (p.5). The political reading is that a third, ideologically fluid splinter coalition may organize the chamber beyond party.
extraction.data: Sample: 19 US House networks, one per two-year session, with session start years 1981 through 2017 (the text also says the study covers 1981 to 2018, p.2). Unit: legislator pairs, each edge signed positive (significantly more co-sponsorships than chance) or negative (significantly fewer). About 445 nodes per network (paper: n ~ 445). Edges: 4,954 to 31,936 (p.4). Source: bill co-sponsorship data, bipartite legislator-bill network, then bipartite projection, then signed backbone (p.7). Ideology: 1st-dimension Nokken-Poole scores from Voteview, -1 liberal to +1 conservative, varying by session (p.8). Effectiveness: Center for Effective Lawmaking scores from 15 indicators, normalized to mean 1 per session (p.8). The paper says code and data are public in the SI (p.8).
extraction.method:
Two binary linear programs, solved to global optimality with Gurobi 9.1 on a 32-core Windows Server VM (p.4). Eq. (1), the k-partition model: binary x_ic assigns node i to cluster c, and f_ij flags frustrated edges. The objective is the minimum frustrated edges for fixed k, C_k(G). Constraints are O(n^2). Eq. (2), a reformulation of the correlation clustering / clique partitioning model (Demaine et al. 2006) for non-complete graphs: binary y_ij marks same-cluster pairs, with constraints over connected triads T. It returns C(G), the minimum over all k, and k*min. Constraints are O(n^3). Signed networks come from the Stochastic Degree Sequence Model in the R backbone package (v1.5.0), with family-wise error alpha = 0.01 via Holm-Bonferroni (p.7-8). Comparison: frustrated-edge counts for party partitions vs optimal k-partitions for k = 2..7. Then coalition mean legislative effectiveness and median ideology, with 95% CI bands (Fig. 4). Analysis is descriptive and per session, with no regression reported.</method>
<parameter name="identification">None in the causal sense. The design is descriptive. The signed network is inferred from co-sponsorship, and optimal partitions are compared with party partitions on frustrated-edge fit. Coalition effectiveness is compared in descriptive plots with CI bands, with no model controlling for party, majority status or committee assignment. The authors discuss the majority-party effect qualitatively (p.6).
extraction.scope: Population: members of the US House of Representatives, sessions starting 1981 through 2017 (text says 1981 to 2018). Institution: the lower chamber only. Era: 1981 to 2018, with contrasts between the 1981-1993 and 2003-2017 sessions (p.5). The optimization methods are general for signed networks up to about 30,000 edges (p.4, p.8). The substantive claims are limited to the House.

key_findings.finding: Globally optimal k-partitions (Eq. 1) and the minimal-k clusterability index (Eq. 2) are computationally feasible for the 19 House networks, up to about 30,000 edges.
key_findings.numbers: Eq. 1 averages 3.3 h; Eq. 2 averages 14 h for networks up to ~30,000 edges. n ~ 445; 4,954 <= m <= 31,936.

key_findings.finding: In every session the party partition leaves more frustrated edges than the optimal 2-partition, which leaves more than the optimal 3-partition. Three coalitions fit the chamber better than two or party.
key_findings.numbers: C_party(G) > C_2(G) > C_3(G) in every session.

key_findings.finding: Beyond k = 3 the frustrated-edge count declines only marginally and then stagnates. For all 19 networks, C(G) = C_k(G) for every k <= 7, so the minimal clusterability index is reached at small k.
The third coalition's size and median ideology vary across sessions, so it is an ideologically fluid group and not a fixed ideological bloc.
key_findings.numbers: Third coalition ranges from 4 members (113th, 2013) to 69 (111th, 2009). Its ideology ranges from very liberal (98th-102nd, 1983-1991) to center-left (103rd, 111th) to center-right (105th-110th, 1997-2007).

key_findings.finding: The third coalition is the most effective coalition in most sessions. Its inclusion explains why the two dominant generalized-balance coalitions are less effective than their party-defined counterparts.
key_findings.numbers: No pooled effect size or test reported; effectiveness is shown as session means with 95% CI bands.

key_findings.finding: Third-coalition effectiveness is anchored by a few very effective members during stable party control. Effectiveness dips during transitions when the majority changes.
key_findings.numbers: 99th-102nd (1985-1990): Pat Williams 4.49, Barney Frank 4.02, Daniel Glickman 3.68. 106th-108th (1999-2004): Christopher Smith 8.44, Bill Young 4.41, Nancy Johnson 2.98. 114th-115th (2015-2018): Edward Royce 5.46, John Katko 5.36, Dave Reichert 2.30.

key_findings.finding: The third coalition has a distinctive sign structure: far more negative (opposition) ties per positive tie, and more of its opposition ties run to co-partisans.
key_findings.numbers: Traditional coalitions: 2.68 negative edges per positive edge. Third coalition: 21.18 (SI Fig. S3). Co-partisan share of negative edges: 8.44% for traditional coalition members, 25.6% for third coalition members.

key_findings.finding: Party, classic balance (k = 2) and generalized balance (k = 3) all show a majority-party effectiveness advantage. The authors attribute this to agenda control and majority vote share. They also say part of the advantage comes from the highly effective third coalition, which is usually ideologically aligned with the majority.
key_findings.numbers: No numerical effect size given for the majority advantage.

key_findings.finding: Party-based coalitions show increasing ideological polarization over time, and classic-balance coalitions look similar. Generalized balance adds a smaller, fluid third group between two diverging dominant coalitions.
key_findings.numbers: No regression or correlation values reported. Descriptive only.

limitations: No dedicated limitations section. In-text caveats: the models can yield multiple optimal solutions, so they do not return a unique partition (p.3-4).

Scale: the models are demonstrated on networks up to about 30,000 edges. The authors call this a minor limitation because many empirical signed networks are sparser, and backbone methods can sparsify dense ones (p.8).
The median ideology of the third coalition is unstable across sessions, so it is not a fixed ideological category (p.7).
Coalition membership 'does not necessarily imply cohesion with other members of the same coalition' (p.5).
The effectiveness comparisons are descriptive plots with 95% CI bands. No controls or inferential tests are reported in the main text (p.6-7).
Signed ties come from a statistical backbone of co-sponsorship, so their validity depends on that inference step (p.7).
measures: Frustrated edges per partition; k-clusterability index C_k(G) for fixed k; C(G) as the minimum over all k; k*min as the smallest k attaining C(G).
Signed co-sponsorship network (SDSM backbone): positive and negative edge counts, and the negative-to-positive ratio per coalition.
Co-partisan share of each member's negative edges.
Ideology: 1st-dimension Nokken-Poole score (Voteview), session-specific, -1 liberal to +1 conservative.
Legislative effectiveness: Center for Effective Lawmaking score (15 indicators, normalized to mean 1 per session), averaged per coalition with 95% CI.

summary_md:
Aref and Neal build signed House networks from co-sponsorship for 19 sessions (1981-2017, about 445 members each). They use an SDSM backbone, so an edge is positive when a pair co-sponsors significantly more than chance and negative when significantly less (alpha .01, Holm). They then solve two binary linear programs to global optimality: the minimum frustrated edges for a fixed k, and the smallest k that reaches the overall minimum. In every session the party split leaves more frustrated edges than the optimal 2-partition, and that leaves more than the optimal 3-partition. k*min runs from 3 to 7, but gains past k=3 are small. The third coalition is small (4 to 69 members) and its ideology shifts from session to session. It is the most effective coalition in most sessions on the CEL LES. It also has an unusual sign pattern: 21.18 negative ties per positive tie, against 2.68 for the two main blocs, and 25.6% of its negative ties go to co-partisans, against 8.44%. All of this is descriptive. There are no controls and no causal design.

What this means for the system as built: `fec/network/signed_coalitions.py` cites this paper but works on a different graph. It partitions the LLM-valenced member-mention layer, which mixes House and Senate and is 83% positive, using a heuristic local search capped at k=3. Its stored artifact (2026-07-19) shows a single main bloc plus a 14-member splinter at k=2. At k=3 the third cluster has one member, and frustration barely moves (1040.79 to 1039.79 weighted). So the system has not reproduced the paper's finding and has not tested it. The paper's real substrate, a signed co-sponsorship backbone, is not built in the live code. The June vote backbone threw away exactly the negative ties that define the third coalition. The CEL LES data is already on disk, so a House-only reproduction is cheap. The finding should stay UNVERIFIED until that reproduction runs.

bearings.paper_claim: The k-partition objective minimizes frustrated edges: negative edges inside a cluster plus positive edges between clusters (Eq. 1, giving C_k(G)). Eq. 2 finds the smallest k that reaches the minimum over all partitions (k*min). Both are solved to global optimality on 19 House networks (n ~445, 4,954 <= m <= 31,936 edges). Eq. 1 averages 3.3 h and Eq. 2 averages 14 h.

bearings.system_side: Uses the same frustration objective, weighted by |net|. It runs a single-node best-move local search with a party seed plus 60 random restarts (SC_RESTARTS), only for k=1..3. The result is an upper bound with no optimality guarantee, and k*min is never searched. No engine or ranking step consumes the output. weekly_refresh.py:522 and refresh_table.py:260 run it as a diagnostic step. However, the member desk surface (make_member_desk.py:826, 1153) reads splinter_k2 and sets an 'antag' flag on members, so the output does reach a display surface. The module docstring's claim that the chain does not consume it is therefore only true for the engine.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The objective transfers directly. The guarantee does not, because local search can stop in a local optimum. At 520 nodes and 7,153 edges the graph has fewer edges than the paper's largest network but slightly more nodes than the paper's n ~445, and the ILP's variable count grows as O(n^2). An exact Eq. 1 run is plausibly feasible but has not been demonstrated at this node count.

bearings.system_side: The signed graph is member_references.json: cross-media mentions, LLM-valenced, with House and Senate mixed (McConnell and Rand Paul appear in the splinter). It has 520 nodes and 7,153 edges (5,959 positive, 1,194 negative). The stored artifact (data/lobbying/signed_coalitions.json, file date 2026-07-19) shows weighted F(1)=1092.31, F(2)<=1040.79 (15.31% of total weight 6,799.18) and F(3)<=1039.79. bearings.transfer_conditions: The evidence does not carry over. Mention valence measures expressed sentiment, while SDSM signs measure collaboration and avoidance against a degree-preserving null. The system's graph also mixes chambers and pools across Congresses, where the paper is House-only and per session. The system's null third-coalition result says nothing for or against the paper. extraction.venue: arXiv preprint arXiv:2505.09617v1 [physics.soc-ph], submitted 22 Mar 2025 (manuscript dated May 16, 2025). No journal venue stated in the text.
extraction.document_type: arXiv preprint; applied mathematics paper presenting a deterministic compartmental ODE model of congressional voting with lobbying and campaign-donation compartments, one simulated case study, stability analysis, and SVM-based sensitivity analysis.
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 1863 lines of C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_text\4e6939c6565d.txt (front matter through the last row of Table 2 on p.33), read in four chunks with nothing skipped. Annotation file C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research\_annots\4e6939c6565d.json read in full: 47 Highlight items on pp.1-23, all with empty author, content and note fields (no sticky notes or comments). Figures 1-18 are known only through their captions and surrounding text; figure images are not in the text file. Some OCR garbling: the p.5 highlight, the nu and tau entries in Table 2 (p.32-33). Metadata hint verified against the text header and title; no correction needed.
extraction.research_question: Can a compartmental differential-equation model of legislators (not yet introduced, undecided centrists, yes, no), extended with lobbyists, lobbying money, and campaign donations, simulate and predict roll-call passage, and how do lobbying and donations change outcomes? Stated objectives (a) build the model, (b) study how interactions shape legislative behavior, (c) predict likelihood of passage (p.3).
extraction.theory: Epidemiology-style mass-action peer influence: undecided legislators (C) move to yes (Y) or no (N) at rates beta_F, beta_A times interactions with Y or N (eqs 2.1a-d, p.4-5). Intro frames lobbying as influence spreading through a network (p.3), but the model itself uses mass action, not a network. Lobbying side: firm value change Delta pi_i = pi*_i - pi0_i; firms with Delta pi > 0 lobby for, < 0 against (Sec 2.1, p.5, following Meng and Rode [17]); lobbying money is split by (1 - psi). Donations drain money M_F, M_A at rates I_F, I_A (eqs 2.2a-h, p.6-7). Authors claim this is the first compartmental-model use of this kind in political science (p.21).
extraction.data: Single case: the 2009 ACESA (American Clean Energy and Security Act, called the Waxman-Markey Bill, p.19) House and Senate votes. Unit: individual legislators in compartments. Population: House S = 435, Senate S = 100 (Table 1, p.19). Lobbyist counts: ProPublica Represent database, ACESA-related lobbyists including former federal employees, 2006-2012 (Sec 2.4 p.9; Fig 3 caption p.9), rising from 0 to about 581 in a logistic-like pattern. Campaign money initial values MF = 345,873,085 and MA = 283,377,397 (Table 1). Parameters in Table 2 (p.32-33) are literature-sourced, e.g., alpha_F(H) 0.449, alpha_A(H) 0.382, alpha_C(H) 0.168 [16]; alpha_F(S) 0.41, alpha_A(S) 0.37, alpha_C(S) 0.22 [16]; nu 5.258e-10 [24]; psi 0.47847 [4]; I_F 345873.09 and I_A 283377.340 [17]; beta_F(H)=beta_A(H)=0.00005425 [7]; beta_F(S)=beta_A(S)=0.000437 [7]; L max = 600 [24][11]. No individual-level or survey data. Sensitivity and SVM runs use 1000 samples per figure (p.14-17). N for the empirical comparison: 435 House and 100 Senate members, one bill.
extraction.method: Deterministic ODE system. Baseline model (eqs 2.1a-d, p.4-5) and extended model with lobbyists L_F, L_A, money M_F, M_A and donations I_F, I_A (eqs 2.2a-h, p.6-7). Well-posedness: positivity via an invariant-domain lemma stated in the text (p.7-8) and boundedness via M(t) = S + C + Y + N constant (p.8). Stability: linearization about (0, C0, 0, 0) (unstable) and (0, 0, Y0, N0) (stable), in Sec 3.1 (p.10) and Sec 3.2.2 (p.12), with closed-form L_F(t), L_A(t) (Sec 3.2.1, p.11). Simulation: no solver, software or numerical tolerance stated. Sensitivity: 10% variation of centrist-flow parameters with distributions of final C, Y, N (Sec 4, p.12-13); parameter sweeps labelled pass/fail and separated by linear SVM (Sec 4.1-4.2, p.14-17); individual parameter impact ranking (Sec 4.3, Fig 12, p.18-19). Ideology sensitivity via centrist band (Sec 5.3, p.20-21). Validation: compare simulated final House and Senate counts to actual tallies using percent error (Sec 5.1, p.19-20).
extraction.identification: None in the econometric sense. No estimation, no quasi-experiment, no causal design. Parameters are fixed from cited literature (Table 2). Validation is a comparison of simulated final vote counts to actual ACESA tallies. The lobbying-on vs lobbying-off contrast (p.19-20) is a simulation contrast under chosen inputs. The abstract says parameters were estimated from public lobbying records and literature, but the text gives no estimation procedure.
extraction.scope: Population: US Congress, the House (435 seats) and Senate (100 seats), one bill, ACESA (2009). Era: lobbying counts 2006-2012 (Fig 3, p.9); the House and Senate votes of 2009 (abstract p.1, Sec 5 p.19). Institution: federal legislature. Authors state that the model has been applied to one bill and that a broader bill set is needed (p.23).

key_findings.finding: Baseline House simulation with no lobbying or donations: model settles at yes/no/undecided counts, compared with actual tally.
key_findings.numbers: Model 230 yes, 196 no, 9 undecided vs actual 219 yes, 212 no, 4 abstain; percent error 5.02% (yes), 7.55% (no).

key_findings.finding: Adding campaign donations alone changes almost nothing; authors conclude donations have limited impact on passage.
key_findings.numbers: 231 yes, 196 no, 8 undecided (one undecided legislator moves to yes).

key_findings.finding: Adding lobbying (with donations) moves the House prediction closer to the actual count; authors attribute the shift mainly to lobbying converting undecided legislators.
key_findings.numbers: 231 yes, 203 no, 1 undecided; percent error 5.48% (yes), 4.25% (no). Undecided fell from 9 to 1, i.e., 8 legislators resolved in total.

key_findings.finding: Senate baseline and extended runs barely differ; authors say lobbying has minimal effect in the Senate, which they read as consistent with ACESA failing against the 60-vote filibuster threshold.
key_findings.numbers: Baseline 52 yes, 47 no, 1 undecided; with lobbying and donations 52 yes, 48 no, 0 undecided. No Senate actual tally is given in the text.

key_findings.finding: Stability: the all-undecided point is unstable; the point with Y and N positive and S, C at zero is stable, so Y and N converge to positive constants and the legislature tends toward a decision. Same qualitative result holds with lobbying and donations included.
key_findings.numbers: No numeric equilibrium values for Y0 or N0 are reported in the text.

key_findings.finding: Sensitivity to a 10% change in centrist flow parameters: final C, Y, N look roughly normally distributed; trajectories cross the actual House vote count, which authors read as robustness.
key_findings.numbers: Parameters varied by 10%; no summary statistics beyond the figures are given in the text.

key_findings.finding: Parameter-impact ranking: centrist-lobbying parameters (M_LF, M_LA) and tau have substantial influence on outcome; initial compartment sizes (S) have minimal impact.
key_findings.numbers: Qualitative ranking only; no effect sizes in the text.

key_findings.finding: SVM pass/fail boundaries: most single-parameter sweeps predict passage; beta and phi matter for passage, tau does not; no clean boundary for the multi-parameter sweeps; authors conclude no simple rate-constant condition guarantees passage.
key_findings.numbers: Linear SVM trained on 1000 samples per figure; red (fail) points lie inside the pass region in Fig 9.

key_findings.finding: Centrist band definition matters: widening the centrist band from -0.25 to 0.25 to -0.35 to 0.35 flips the House result so that no votes exceed yes votes.
key_findings.numbers: Band +/-0.25 vs +/-0.35 on a -1 to 1 ideology scale; the flipped vote counts are not given in the text.

key_findings.finding: ACESA lobbyist counts rise from 0 toward about 581 in a logistic-like pattern over 2006-2012.
key_findings.numbers: Upper bound approximately 581 lobbyists; Table 2 uses L max = 600 (p.33).

key_findings.finding: Introduction context (cited to Meng and Rode [17], not produced by this paper's model): lobbying accounted for 14% of lobbying expenditures in the period, and lobbyists reduced the likelihood of ACESA passage by about 13%.
key_findings.numbers: 14% of lobbying expenditures; about 13% reduction in passage likelihood (cited).

limitations: Single bill (ACESA) with one validation point per chamber; the authors themselves say the model should be applied to a broader set of bills (Sec 6, p.23).

Headline claim vs own numbers: the Introduction says the model predicts roll-call outcomes 'within 5% of the actual results' (p.3). Positivity relies on an invariant-domain lemma stated without proof (p.7). Table 2 OCR is garbled for tau (value text '000000001112433819', p.33) and for nu; treat those entries as unverified.
The network framing (p.3, p.23) is not modeled: peer influence is mass action and no network data are used.

summary_md:
Jacoby et al. (arXiv 2505.09617, 2025) model a legislature the way an epidemic model tracks a population. Each legislator sits in one of four compartments: not yet introduced (S), undecided centrist (C), yes (Y) or no (N). Undecided members move to Y or N through mass-action contact with members who have already decided. The extended model adds lobbyist counts and lobbying money (L_F, L_A, M_F, M_A) and drains campaign donations (I_F, I_A). Every parameter is fixed from earlier literature (Table 2); none is estimated. The model is checked against one bill, the 2009 Waxman-Markey vote (ACESA).

In the House, the baseline run gives 230 yes, 196 no and 9 undecided, against an actual 219 to 212. Adding donations moves 1 member. Adding lobbying resolves 8 more undecided members (231 yes, 203 no, 1 undecided). The Senate barely changes. The analysis shows that the centrist-flow and centrist-lobbying parameters (M_LF, M_LA) drive the outcome. An SVM finds no clean pass/fail boundary. Widening the centrist ideology band from ±0.25 to ±0.35 reverses the House result.

For Paul's system this is weak evidence. Each chamber has one comparison point, every "effect" is the output of parameters the authors chose, and the paper's claim of accuracy within 5% does not hold against its own errors of 5.02%, 5.48% and 7.55%. Its useful content is structural, not empirical:
- Legislators who have already decided are treated as fixed, and only undecided members move. This matches the low PERS values for Champion and Opponent.
- Who counts as movable decides the result. The system already found the same thing when it swept PERS_NONE.
- The sensitivity harness does not sweep the flip model's WM/WP channel weights or the PERS table. The paper says centrist-flow parameters are the ones that matter, so those are the obvious next sweeps.

The lobbying-versus-donations contrast should not be imported into the flip model. It is a contrast between simulation runs, not an estimate. Its lobbyist counts also come from revolving-door staff, and project rules bar LDA as an edge or weight source (D-021).

bearings.paper_claim: Varying the centrist-flow parameters by 10% produces a wide spread of final C, Y and N counts. In the parameter-impact ranking, centrist-lobbying parameters (M_LF, M_LA) and tau rank high and initial compartment sizes rank low. Linear SVMs on 1000-sample sweeps find no clean pass/fail boundary in multi-parameter sweeps.
bearings.system_side: The receptivity sensitivity harness sweeps only receptivity constants: susc scale, prospect-theory multipliers, retiring factor and persona weight (VARIANTS). It grades each by top-20 overlap (ROBUST at 18 or more). The harness does not sweep the flip model's channel weights WM/WP (0.35/0.65) or the PERS persuadability table. The one centrist-like knob that has been swept, PERS_NONE, was swept by hand and recorded in a comment: top-20 overlap was 16/18/20/18/15 across 0.30-0.95, and total winnability ran from 149.5 to 245.8.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The transfer is a method idea, not evidence. Jacoby's sensitivity comes from a well-mixed ODE model with literature-fixed parameters, and the system's flip model is a network-based ratio of saturating terms. What carries over is the diagnostic: the parameters that decide who is movable and how fast they move should be swept first. The pass/fail SVM is not needed, because top-k overlap already measures decision change. Any such sweep is a bound on the model, not validation (DE-062).
bearings.verifier_note: Paper: 10% variation of centrist-flow parameters (p.12, Fig 4 caption); Fig 12 text names M_LF, M_LA and tau as substantial and initial compartment size S as minimal (p.18-19); linear SVMs trained on 1000 samples, no boundary found for phi (Fig 10) and tau (Fig 11), misclassified points for beta (Fig 9) (p.16). The paper itself calls the model 'robust to moderate changes' (p.13); 'wide spread' is the analyst's reading of 'more significant variability'. Code: VARIANTS at receptivity_sensitivity.py:92-102 are the listed receptivity constants, verdict thresholds 18/15 at :111; a separate seed_prob coefficient sweep (:118 on) is also receptivity-layer, graded by gate analytics. No WM/WP/PERS sweep in the file. PERS_NONE comment with 16/18/20/18/15 and 149.5->245.8 at flip_model.py:22-27.

bearings.paper_claim: Only undecided centrists (C) move. Committed Y and N legislators are absorbing states, and the equilibrium with all members undecided is unstable. Widening the centrist band on a -1 to 1 ideology scale from ±0.25 to ±0.35 reverses the House result so that no votes exceed yes votes.
bearings.system_side: PERS assigns committed tiers near-zero persuadability (Champion 0.10, Defender 0.12, Opponent 0.08) and middle tiers the highest (Highly Persuadable 0.65). Silent members get PERS_NONE 0.45; per the flip_model comment, silent cells are 59.8% of matrix cells. Tiers are based on stance, not ideology.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports the extremes being near-fixed only because its model assumes it; Y and N are absorbing by construction. It does not test an inverted-U. Its centrist group is defined by an unnamed ideology scale, while PERS is defined by CU stance tier, so the band result carries over only as a warning: how the movable set is defined can decide the outcome. The system's PERS_NONE sweep shows the same thing in the system itself. Evidence is a single bill (ACESA, 2009) at the federal level.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper side holds: Y and N equations have only inflows (p.4-5), the (0,C0,0,0) equilibrium is stated unstable (Sec 3.1), and the ±0.25 to ±0.35 band change yields no > yes (p.21, Fig 18). Code side holds for PERS values (moneyball_core.py:565-568), but the 'about 60% of cells' figure lives in the flip_model.py:22 comment, not the cited moneyball_core lines; code_ref extended and Defender 0.12 added.

bearings.paper_claim: With parameters taken from cited literature and databases (none fitted to the vote), adding donations to the House run moves 1 legislator (230 to 231 yes, 8 undecided). The lobbying run yields 231 yes, 203 no, 1 undecided; the authors describe this as undecided members falling from 9 to 1 and conclude that lobbying sways undecided members more than donations do.
bearings.system_side: pflip = a/(a+b), with a saturating FEC-money term weighted WM 0.35 and a peer-proximity term weighted WP 0.65. Money is treated as the minority channel. The model has no lobbying-contact channel; money means campaign receipts only.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Directionally consistent with the claim that money moves votes little, but this is a contrast between simulation runs under chosen inputs, not an estimated effect. The firm-value inputs (rho_Y, rho_N, Delta pi) are not reported in Table 2, the effect is 7-8 of 435 members on one bill (House, ACESA 2009), and the lobbying input is a ProPublica count of all ACESA-related lobbyists (regular plus a revolving-door subgroup, Fig 3 caption). The paper gives no basis for setting WM/WP or for adding a lobbying channel. Under D-021, LDA-derived lobbying data cannot become an edge or weight term.

The paper does not say whether the lobbying run also includes donations; 'resolves 8 of 9' is the authors' 9->1 framing, while versus the donations run it is 7. Original transfer_conditions called the lobbying input 'a count of revolving-door lobbyists'; the Fig 3 caption says it includes both regular lobbyists and a revolving-door subgroup, corrected. 'Literature-fixed' corrected: alpha rates from Voteview [16], nu and L from ProPublica [24]. Code lines 21 and 92-96 confirmed.

The Senate is reported only for the combined lobbying-plus-donations run, which changes it by one senator (52/47/1 to 52/48/0). The authors note that donations may reflect ideology rather than buy influence (citing Bonica [5]).

bearings.transfer_conditions: This is a consistency check, not a calibration. The donation effect in the paper is a model output from literature parameters (I_F, I_A taken from Meng and Rode), not an observed shift. summary_issues: 'Adding lobbying resolves 8 more undecided members' implies 9 resolved after the donations step; the paper frames the lobbying run as 9 -> 1 undecided relative to baseline, which is 7 more than the donations run (8 undecided). The paper does not state whether the lobbying run includes donations.

'Every parameter is fixed from earlier literature (Table 2)' is loose: alpha rates come from Voteview [16], nu and L from ProPublica [24], others from cited papers. The accurate statement is that none is fitted to the ACESA vote.

'Its lobbyist counts also come from revolving-door staff' is wrong: the Fig 3 caption says the series includes both regular lobbyists and a revolving-door subgroup. The same error appears in the flags ('counts former federal employees, i.e. revolving-door staff') and in the flip-model bearing's transfer_conditions.

The accuracy critique lists errors 5.02%, 5.48% and 7.55% but omits the 4.25% no-vote error in the lobbying run, which is within 5%; the 'within 5%' claim fails for 3 of the 4 reported House errors, not all of them.

'Legislators who have already decided are treated as fixed ... This matches the low PERS values' presents a model assumption (Y and N absorbing by construction) as agreement; it is structural similarity, not support.
The Bonica related link was labeled 'cites', but Jacoby cites a different Bonica paper, not the 2013 vault item.

paul_alignment speaks of Paul's highlights and notes, but paul_entries is empty and the 47 annotations have empty content fields; only highlighted spans exist, so claims about what Paul's notes record or omit are not verifiable.
gaps_exposed: The receptivity sensitivity harness sweeps only receptivity constants (fec/members/receptivity_sensitivity.py:93-103). It does not sweep the flip model's WM/WP channel split (flip_model.py:21) or the PERS tier values (moneyball_core.py:564-568), which are the system's equivalents of the centrist-flow parameters the paper finds dominant. PERS_NONE was swept once by hand and the result exists only as a code comment.

The system has no test of how the movable set is defined. PERS assigns persuadability by stance-tier label, and nothing measures how much targeting changes when tier cutpoints move. The paper's centrist-band reversal (±0.25 to ±0.35) shows that the band definition alone can decide the outcome.

The paper's whole premise is a timeline of how members move from undecided to decided, and the system has no outcome check of that kind. The prospective contract (H1/H2) is the planned check, but its F5 power gate is underpowered (72 of the 150 required new-event members).
flags: The lobbying-versus-donations finding must not be used to add a lobbying channel or weight to the flip model. Its lobbying input is a count of ACESA-related lobbyists, and LDA is an identity source only, not an edge or weight source (D-021).
The paper's lobbyist series counts former federal employees, i.e. revolving-door staff (Sec 2.4, p.9). Any summary must not describe those ties with influence language.

The paper's headline accuracy claim ('within 5%', p.3) is contradicted by its own errors (5.02% and 7.55% at baseline; 5.48% yes with lobbying). If quoted, name the window and denominator: one bill (ACESA 2009), House N=435, one comparison per chamber, parameters not estimated.
Any SVM boundary or parameter-impact ranking from the paper describes the model, not legislators. If adapted here, the result stays UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).
The paper frames lobbying as influence spreading through a network (p.3), but the model is well-mixed mass action with no network. Do not cite it as network-diffusion evidence for the cascade kernel.
paul_alignment: Paul's highlights accurately reflect what the paper reports: lobbying moves undecided members more than donations do, outcomes are highly sensitive to centrist-flow parameters, and centrists shift under outside pressure. His notes do not record how thin the evidence is. It is one bill, every parameter is fixed from earlier literature, the lobbying effect is 8 legislators resolved out of 435, and the paper's 5% accuracy claim fails against its own numbers. Read correctly, the paper is consistent with the system's stance that money buys access more than votes (WM 0.35 < WP 0.65; MAXSHIFT 18) and with near-fixed extremes in PERS. It gives no basis for the specific values. Pairing it in his notes with Paul's ROI enthusiasm overstates it. His sensitivity highlight is the most actionable part and is not stale: the system bounds receptivity constants but has not swept its own centrist-flow analogues (WM/WP and the PERS tiers). The lobbying channel he highlighted (green) cannot be built from LDA under D-021.

related.why: Jacoby cites Bonica's roll-call inference paper [5], not the 2013 paper, for the claim that donations may reflect ideology rather than influence (p.20). The 2013 paper is Paul's on-disk anchor for that ideological-money reading but is not itself cited, so the relation is complements, not cites.

Kalla and Broockman provide experimental evidence that money buys access. Jacoby's finding that donations barely move votes is a simulated parallel with no causal design, and Kalla is the stronger basis for the flip model's WM < WP. Not cited by Jacoby.

Jacoby cites Kim and Kunisky [14] in its list of data sources used to predict voting outcomes (p.2-3), not for the network framing (the p.3 network sentence is uncited), and does not model a network. Kim and Kunisky is the actual lobbying-network treatment.

Jacoby cites Poole and Rosenthal [19] for spatial models and Voteview [16] for the alpha rates (Table 2). This vault item (D-NOMINATE after 10 years) is not itself cited; the centrist-band reversal plausibly depends on that kind of ideal-point scale, though the paper does not name the scale it used.
Jacoby's sensitivity runs are deterministic sweeps of 1000 samples. Monte Carlo practice is the stochastic extension the authors say would enhance the model (p.22). Not cited by Jacoby.

Furnas et al. separate lobbying from PAC spending at the organization level. Jacoby's lobbying-versus-donations split rests on parameter choices, not on data that separates the two channels. Not cited by Jacoby.

summary_md:
**What the paper is.** This is a short Cambridge Elements methods tutorial on collecting and processing Twitter data for social scientists. The excerpt on disk covers printed pages 1-10 only and stops partway through section 2.1.1. There is no estimator, no test and no causal design. Its content is descriptive figures from 2016 and a description of the data pipes:
- **Scale:** 319M monthly active users and about 500M tweets a day.
- **US adult usage:** 24% use Twitter; 42% of users use it daily.
- **Elite coverage:** every Senator and 430 House members have official accounts.
- **Geotags:** geotagged tweets are about 2-3% of traffic and skew urban and higher-income.
- **Access limits:** the streaming API gives about a 1% sample with no information on the author's network. The REST API caps each account at its 3,200 most recent tweets and is needed to rebuild follower networks. Author metadata reflects the time of the API request, not the time the tweet was posted.

The rest of the excerpt compares R packages (streamR, twitteR, RCurl) with Python packages (twython, tweepy, pandas). Network analysis is deferred to a separate 2016 work by the same author.

**Why it matters here, and how little.** The system's social channel does not use the Twitter API at all. X, Facebook and Truth Social posts come from a licensed Quorum export; Bluesky posts are collected directly. The social network layer is built from reposts and @mentions found in post text, not from follower or friend lists. So the 3,200-tweet cap, the rate limits and the stream-sampling limits do not bind on the system as built.

Two points do carry over, both as context:
- **Coverage:** the elite-coverage figure supports the assumption that nearly every member has a social channel to read, though the figure is from 2016.
- **Metadata timing:** handle-to-member mapping and attribution happen at collection time. This is a provenance caveat for the member-attributed corpus.

Research questions and gaps Paul states:
1. Conversion step. Birkenmaier and Lechner, Peng et al., and Ramey et al. each say the pipeline does not specify how a model's output becomes a graph node or vector. This is the most repeated gap in the document.

4. Temporal lag. Kim et al. are reactive, not predictive, because filing reports lag current positions.
5. Model limits. Peng et al. say long-distance dependency is the main obstacle for most emotion models; stacking reduces but does not remove it.
6. Venue coverage. Ramey et al. offer no pipeline for textual venues beyond their own, and Paul says a framework for contextual or auditory constraints is also needed.

extraction.title: Image as Data: Automated Content Analysis for Visual Presentations of Political Actors and Events
extraction.document_type: Journal article (open access, CC BY 4.0), with lettered appendices A-G and references. Metadata hint corrected: authors are Jungseock Joo (UCLA Communication) and Zachary C. Steinert-Threlkeld (UCLA Public Policy); the hint's title and year were correct; full DOI and page range added.
extraction.coverage: Read all 2,595 lines of the extracted text (front matter through references and appendices A-G) and all 65 items in the annotation JSON. Page mapping: annotation "page" = PDF page; printed journal page = PDF page + 10. Covered text in the annotations is raw PDF extraction, so two-column lines are interleaved and some items are fragments; the trimmed covered text below is cut to roughly the first 25 words. Lobbying, network analysis, path-finding and resource allocation do not appear in the paper. Elections, persuasion and turnout appear only as literature background and in the vote-choice and mobilization claims (printed p.14-15). Text measurement appears only as contrast (Appendix A, printed p.36-38).
extraction.research_question: Can large-scale image data be analyzed with deep learning / convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to measure political communication that text methods and small manual codings cannot reach? Two applied questions: (1) how U.S. politicians' Facebook photographs differ by party and gender, measured with an off-the-shelf label API; (2) how protest images shared on Twitter frame events, with testable expectations that protest images emphasize state violence over protester violence (H1) and crowds over individuals (H2).
extraction.theory: Visual information is processed more easily and emotionally than text (Graber 1996; Grabe and Bucy 2009); the visual cue may dominate when visual and verbal cues conflict (Gibson and Zillmann 2000); images are information shortcuts for complex issues (Popkin 1994). Ideology predicts object emphasis (conservative: nationalism, capitalism; liberal: inequality reduction); gender predicts self-presentation of physical features (Carpinella et al. 2016; Bauer and Carpinella 2018). Protest framing: frames affect recruitment (Benford and Snow 2000); protester violence reduces support while state violence increases it, so protesters should emphasize state violence (H1); crowds lower individual risk and create mobilization feedback, so protesters should emphasize crowds (H2) (Moore 1995; Biggs 2016).
extraction.identification: None causal. Study 1: descriptive chi-squared association between party (or gender-by-party) and label presence, no controls, no multiple-comparison correction reported. Study 2: descriptive comparison of duplication rates across events and labels, no inferential statistics; hypothesis check is by comparing rates within events (H1 state vs protester violence; H2 group vs child/faces).
extraction.data: Study 1: 15,647 public Facebook photographs (timeline, mobile and profile albums, via the Graph API) posted by 677 candidates in the 2018 U.S. general election, Aug 5 to Nov 6, 2018. Unit = photograph (candidate-level sample; candidate list from Wikipedia, accounts identified manually). Each photo was sent to Google's Label Detection API; 1,730 unique labels were returned. Per-party and per-gender Ns are not stated in the main text. Study 2: geolocated tweets and their images from five protest episodes: Catalonia (Spain, secessionist, 2017), Hong Kong (2014, electoral reform), Russia (anti-corruption, 26 Mar 2017), South Korea (2016-17, Park Geun-hye), and Venezuela (2014-15), printed p.31-33 and footnote 5. Tweets were not keyword-filtered. The analysis sample N is not stated in the main text. Protest-image classifier training set: 32,611 images (Appendix D, printed p.48-50 and Fig. D1/D2 captions). Training images were a mixture of Google Image results and geolocated tweet images.
extraction.method: Study 1: off-the-shelf Google Vision Label Detection (no training); label prevalence by party computed as the share of images with each label (pD, pR); chi-squared test per label, separate for male and female candidates; labels sorted by chi-square (Tables 1-2, printed p.28-29). Unsupervised check: ImageNet-pretrained CNN features (2,048-dim penultimate layer), k-means with k=200 (Appendix F, printed p.54-55). Study 2: fine-tuned ResNet-50 (He et al. 2016) for protest image classification and for violence/police/fire/sign labels; FairFace classifier (Karkkainen and Joo 2019) for face sex, race and age; six frame labels (contains child, faces, large group, small group, protester violence, state violence); duplicate detection via cosine-style pairwise distance on the 1,000-dim last fully connected layer, duplicate if normalized distance below 0.2 (threshold chosen by inspecting the histogram); framing rate = share of duplicate images within each event-label (Table 3, printed p.33). Background sections describe CNN architecture, transfer learning, training, validation (Grad-CAM visualization, Appendix D) and ethics. Table D1 compares architectures (AlexNet, VGG-16/19, ResNet-18/34/50) for protest fine-tuning.
extraction.scope: Population: candidates in the 2018 U.S. general election (Facebook photos) and protest-related Twitter images from five protest episodes in Catalonia, Hong Kong, Russia, South Korea and Venezuela (2014-2017). Institutions: U.S. elections and social-media platforms. Era: 2014 to 2018 data, published 2022. The paper is a methods tutorial with two applications, so the external validity of the substantive findings is explicitly limited.

limitations: Authors call the Study 2 results provisional and say they are not a definitive answer (printed p.33, PDF p.23).

Framing is operationalized only as percentage duplicated images; the authors suggest counts of tweets and more frames as alternatives (printed p.34).
Study 2 uses a duplicate threshold of 0.2 chosen by inspecting one histogram; no sensitivity analysis is reported (printed p.32).
Google's Vision API architecture and training data are not published; the authors recommend validating API labels against manual annotations (footnote 2, printed p.57).
Labels inherit model and data bias; Google's gender label for photographs in image search underrepresents women relative to occupational share, as cited (Lam et al. 2018) (printed p.23-24).
Pretrained classifiers and APIs have inferior customizability; custom concepts require new annotated training data (printed p.30).

Interpretability: deep models have millions of parameters; validation relies on accuracy metrics plus visualization (Grad-CAM), which the authors say does not explain how the model reaches its output (printed p.51-53).
Privacy and consent: face detection can identify protesters, so researchers should not release identifiable photographs and should seek IRB approval for social-media image studies (printed p.24).
The paper does not report accuracy of the six frame labels in the main text; the verification it cites (Appendix G) is Grad-CAM visualization only (printed p.56).
Study 1 reports no multiple-comparison correction across roughly 1,700 labels; significance stars are per-label chi-squared tests (Tables 1-2).

summary_md:
Joo and Steinert-Threlkeld (CCR 2022) is a methods tutorial on treating images as data, with two applications. Study 1 sends 15,647 Facebook photos from 677 candidates in 2018 through Google's label API. It runs chi-squared tests of label against party separately by gender, because the parties' gender ratios differ. Republican men over-index labels like Official and Military officer. Republican women over-index Blond and Red. There is no correction for testing about 1,700 labels. Study 2 fine-tunes a ResNet-50 (91.79% accuracy) on protest images from five protest episodes. It defines framing as the share of near-duplicate images per event and frame label, where a duplicate is a normalized feature distance below 0.2, a threshold picked from one histogram. H1 (state violence shared more than protester violence) and H2 (crowds shared more than individuals) each hold in 3 of 5 events. The authors call the results provisional. There is no causal identification.

For Paul's systems, the paper matters in one place. fec/network/frame_alignment.py ports both instruments to text: near-duplicate press titles across members (3-word-shingle Jaccard >= 0.5), and chi-squared category and term association with party. Checking the code showed that the transfer breaks on the unit of analysis. Joo's sharer chooses the image. The text port reads cu_press_stance_tone.csv with no source filter, and 816 of its 2,388 rows are americascreditunions.org articles that are attributed to each member they mention. One ACU headline credited to many members therefore counts as members echoing one script. In a single-path recompute that is UNVERIFIED under DE-062, General CU duplication falls from 60.2% (n=442) to 5.2% (n=116), and CU Tax Status from 64.7% (n=190) to 38.1% (n=42), once only *.senate.gov and *.house.gov rows are kept. The output is a diagnostic, last written 2026-07-01. It reaches salience_shock only under `--intensity auto`, and the chain does not pass that flag.

Overarching argument: Paul treats machine learning and NLP applied to public political text (congressional floor speech, public statements, lobbying filings) as a way to produce actor-level attributes (personality traits, policy positions, emotion) that can be placed on nodes of a social-network-analysis graph. The purpose he names is political intelligence: lobbying strategy, industry alignment, and how to pitch policy to a specific member of Congress.

Research questions and gaps Paul states:
1. Conversion step. Birkenmaier and Lechner, Peng et al., and Ramey et al. each say the pipeline does not specify how a model's output becomes a graph node or vector. This is the most repeated gap in the document.
2. Ambiguity. Birkenmaier and Lechner say the method does not separate ambiguous statements.
3. Conflict. Kim et al. do not show inter-industry conflict over a specific bill, which Paul says matters for political intelligence.
4. Temporal lag. Kim et al. are reactive, not predictive, because filing reports lag current positions.
5. Model limits. Peng et al. say long-distance dependency is the main obstacle for most emotion models; stacking reduces but does not remove it.
6. Venue coverage. Ramey et al. offer no pipeline for textual venues beyond their own, and Paul says a framework for contextual or auditory constraints is also needed.

Synthesis: Birkenmaier and Lechner and Ramey et al. both concern personality measurement from speech or text, with Ramey et al. as the older foundation and Birkenmaier and Lechner as the newer, codebook-backed method. Kim et al. and Birkenmaier and Lechner both concern the actor-to-graph link. Peng et al. supplies the model landscape that the other two would run on.
